title: THEY SOLD A LITTLE GIRL FOR WINE—AND HEAVEN DID NOT STAY SILENT.
paragraphs: THEY SOLD A LITTLE GIRL FOR WINE—AND HEAVEN DID NOT STAY SILENT.
Why God condemned those who treated children as objects to be traded—and what His judgment reveals about a world that has forgotten the value of a human soul.
Imagine being a child in a world where your life was worth less than someone else's moment of pleasure.
No one asked your name.
No one cared about your dreams, your fears, or the family you desperately wanted to see again.
Your tears could not change the transaction.
Someone looked at you, calculated your value, and decided what they could get in exchange for your life.
And somewhere, someone drank wine purchased at the cost of a little girl's freedom.
This is not a fictional horror story.
It is written in Scripture.
“And they have cast lots for my people; and have given a boy for an harlot, and sold a girl for wine, that they might drink.” — Joel 3:3 (KJV)
Read that last sentence again.
They sold a girl for wine, that they might drink.
An entire human life exchanged for temporary satisfaction.
A child created in the image of God reduced to a transaction.
A future stolen so that someone else could satisfy an appetite.
And God saw everything.

There are passages in Scripture that comfort us. There are passages that encourage us. And then there are passages that should make us put down our phones, examine our hearts, and ask what kind of humanity we have become.
Joel 3:3 is one of them.
In the original Biblical Hebrew, which numbers this passage as Joel 4:3, we encounter these devastating words:
וַיִּתְּנוּ הַיֶּלֶד בַּזּוֹנָה וְהַיַּלְדָּה מָכְרוּ בַיַּיִן וַיִּשְׁתּוּ
Vayyittenu hayyeled bazzonah, vehayyaldah makheru vayyayin vayyishtu.
A close translation reads:
“They gave the boy in exchange for a prostitute, and the girl they sold for wine, and they drank.”
The Hebrew word יֶלֶד (yeled) refers to a boy or child, while יַלְדָּה (yaldah) refers to a girl.
The verb מָכְרוּ (makheru) means “they sold.”
This was not simply a metaphor for disrespect. The passage describes human beings being treated as commodities.
The final Hebrew expression, וַיִּשְׁתּוּ (vayyishtu), means “and they drank.”
The transaction was completed. The wine was consumed.
The perpetrators enjoyed the proceeds of their cruelty.
But the God of heaven did not forget the children.

To understand the weight of this passage, we must understand its context. In Joel 3:1–8, God announces judgment against nations responsible for scattering His people, dividing His land, plundering their possessions, and selling the people of Judah and Jerusalem into slavery.
The passage specifically addresses Tyre, Sidon, and the regions of Philistia.
These were not innocent commercial exchanges. They were acts of exploitation committed against vulnerable people.
God declared that He would bring these nations into judgment.
Why?
Because what the world considered profitable, God considered worthy of judgment.
What people treated as merchandise, God called “my people.”
Those two words change everything.
The children had not become worthless because someone placed a price on them.
Their dignity had not disappeared because someone refused to recognize it.
Their suffering had not become insignificant because powerful people benefited from it.
God still saw them.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that today.
What someone did to you does not determine what you are worth.
You may have been treated as an inconvenience, an object, a source of income, a means of gratification, or a burden someone wanted to discard.
Perhaps your childhood was spent surviving things you were too young to understand.
Perhaps the people who should have protected you became the very people you needed protection from.
Perhaps you learned to smile in public because nobody seemed interested in what happened behind closed doors.
You grew older.
But some memories never grew old.
Some wounds followed you into adulthood, into relationships, into marriage, into parenthood, and even into church.
And sometimes, in the silence, you wondered whether God had noticed.
Joel reminds us that human cruelty does not escape divine attention.
God's awareness does not mean every injustice will be resolved immediately in this life. Scripture never promises that the innocent will be spared every earthly sorrow.
But it does assure us that evil is not invisible to Him.
“The LORD executeth righteousness and judgment for all that are oppressed.” — Psalm 103:6 (KJV)
The foundation of this truth begins long before Joel.
Genesis 1:27 declares that humanity was created in the image of God.
The Hebrew expression בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים (betselem Elohim) means “in the image of God.”
Human dignity is not something society invents.
It is something God establishes.
A child's worth does not depend on intelligence, appearance, nationality, economic status, usefulness, disability, or the circumstances surrounding their birth.
Children are not possessions to exploit.
They are not instruments for adult gratification.
They are not disposable obstacles to personal ambition.
They are human beings bearing the image of their Creator.
And when Jesus Christ entered our broken world, He revealed the heart of God toward those whom society frequently overlooked.
In Mark 10:13–16, people brought little children to Jesus so that He might touch them. His disciples rebuked those bringing them.
But Jesus was displeased.
The Greek word used in Mark 10:14 is ἠγανάκτησεν (ēganaktēsen), meaning that He became indignant.
Jesus was not indifferent when children were being pushed away.
He cared enough to confront the people standing between them and Him.
“Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.” — Mark 10:14 (KJV)
Then He took them into His arms and blessed them.
Consider the contrast.
In Joel, children were handed over for someone else's pleasure.
In Mark, children were welcomed into the arms of the Savior.
One reveals the corruption of the human heart.
The other reveals the compassion of Christ.
One reduces children to their usefulness.
The other receives them with love.
And the distance between those two pictures should force every Christian to examine how seriously we take the protection of the vulnerable.
Because the spirit of exploitation did not disappear when the ancient world ended.
Human trafficking still exists.
Children are still exploited through forced labor, sexual abuse, coercion, and commercial exploitation.
Some are manipulated by people they trust.
Some are silenced to protect family reputations.
Some are failed by institutions more concerned about their public image than the people entrusted to their care.
Some cry for help in ways adults dismiss as misbehavior.
And sometimes the most dangerous place for a child is the place everyone assumes is safe.

The International Labour Organization, Walk Free, and the International Organization for Migration estimated in their 2022 Global Estimates of Modern Slavery report that approximately 3.3 million children were in forced labor in 2021.
Behind every statistic is a human being.
A name.
A face.
A childhood that should have been protected.
The tragedy is not merely that exploitation exists.
It is that people can become so accustomed to hearing about it that they stop feeling anything.
We scroll.
We sigh.
We shake our heads.
And then we move on.
But what happens when our ability to move on becomes greater than our willingness to care?
Proverbs 31:8–9 calls us to speak for those who cannot adequately defend themselves and to uphold the rights of the poor and needy.
Biblical compassion is not merely feeling sorry for someone.
It is love willing to act.

Protecting children means listening when they disclose harm, taking credible concerns seriously, reporting suspected abuse through appropriate safeguarding and legal authorities, and refusing to conceal wrongdoing simply because the accused person is respected, influential, related to us, or religious.
A church that protects its reputation at the expense of an abused child has profoundly misunderstood the heart of Christ.
Forgiveness must never become an excuse for concealment.
Grace must never become permission for continued abuse.
And reconciliation must never be demanded at the expense of a victim's safety.
The Gospel does not require survivors to return to dangerous situations to prove their faith.
Jesus never taught us to protect evil from accountability.
He taught us to walk in truth.
And yet, the uncomfortable reality of Scripture is that it does not allow us merely to condemn the sins of others while ignoring our own hearts.
We may never have sold a child for wine.
But have we ever treated another person's suffering as less important than our convenience?
Have we ever remained silent because speaking the truth might cost us something?
Have we ever cared more about maintaining appearances than confronting wrongdoing?
Have we ever defended someone simply because we loved them, even when their behavior harmed someone vulnerable?
Have we ever looked away because the problem was not happening inside our own home?
Sin often survives because people decide that confronting it is too inconvenient.
And that is where Joel stops being merely an ancient prophecy and becomes a mirror.
The Bible exposes not only the cruelty of human actions but also the corruption of the heart from which those actions emerge.
Jesus said in Mark 7:21–23 that evil thoughts and sinful actions proceed from within the human heart.
Our greatest problem is deeper than broken systems.
It is humanity's rebellion against God.
And our greatest hope is not merely better behavior.
It is redemption through Jesus Christ.
At the center of the Christian faith stands another terrible transaction.
Judas agreed to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:14–16).
The sinless Son of God was betrayed for money.
He was rejected, mocked, condemned, and crucified.
The One through whom all things were created entered a world where human beings repeatedly placed prices on lives they did not own.
Yet Jesus willingly gave Himself for sinners.
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” — Mark 10:45 (KJV)
The Greek word translated as ransom is λύτρον (lytron), referring to a ransom or price of release.
Notice the extraordinary reversal.
Sin sacrifices others to satisfy itself.
Christ sacrificed Himself to redeem others.
Human greed asks, “What can I gain from your life?”
Jesus declares, through the cross, what He willingly gave to accomplish our redemption.
First Peter 1:18–19 reminds believers that they were redeemed not with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
The cross is not God's indifference toward evil.
It reveals both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable depth of divine mercy.
And the resurrection declares that sin and death will not have the final word.
This is why the Gospel is not merely a message for people with respectable histories.
It is hope for the wounded.
Hope for the forgotten.
Hope for those carrying shame that was never theirs to bear.
And even hope for guilty sinners who genuinely repent, turn from their wickedness, and place their faith in Jesus Christ.
But genuine repentance does not demand immunity from consequences.
Zacchaeus demonstrated the fruit of repentance through restitution in Luke 19:8–9.
A transformed heart does not ask how much wrongdoing it can conceal beneath the language of grace.
It comes into the light.
It accepts accountability.
It seeks to repair what can be repaired.
It turns away from the sin it once defended.
That is the difference between using Christianity as a hiding place and surrendering to Jesus as Lord.
Perhaps you are reading this with a wound nobody knows about.
Perhaps you were once the child whose voice was ignored.
Perhaps you are a parent terrified by the kind of world your children are growing up in.
Perhaps you are recognizing moments when you should have spoken but remained silent.
Whatever brought you here, do not leave this truth behind when you close your screen.
Bring your pain, your fears, your failures, and your need for healing before Christ.
Seek trustworthy support when you need it. Professional care, safeguarding, and legal protection are not enemies of faith.
You do not have to disclose painful personal experiences publicly to prove your courage or your relationship with God.
Let the comments become a place of prayer, compassion, and encouragement rather than judgment.

That simple act can help biblical truth reach someone beyond our immediate community—perhaps someone silently struggling, a parent who needs encouragement, a believer who has become indifferent, or someone who has never understood the compassionate heart of Jesus.
Let us build a community that does more than consume Christian content.
Let us become people who live what we believe.
People who defend the vulnerable.
People who refuse to excuse darkness.
People who proclaim repentance without abandoning compassion, and preach grace without compromising truth.
Ministry requires more than words. Continuing and expanding this work requires time, resources, commitment, and the generosity of people who believe biblical truth should reach more souls.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), while reminding us that giving must come from a willing heart rather than compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
You cannot purchase God's favor.
You cannot buy salvation.
And if you cannot give financially, never believe that your prayers, encouragement, and willingness to share are insignificant.
There are many ways to serve Christ faithfully.
The purpose is not to build a name for ourselves.
It is to make the name of Jesus known.
Because somewhere, someone still believes that what happened to them has permanently destroyed their worth.
Somewhere, a wounded adult is still carrying the grief of a frightened child.
Somewhere, a person needs to hear that the God who condemned the exploitation recorded in Joel is the same God whose Son welcomed children into His arms.
And somewhere, a believer needs to remember that following Jesus means refusing to become comfortable with the suffering of others.
Joel 3:3 records a world in which people exchanged children for fleeting pleasure.
The Gospel reveals a Savior who willingly gave His life to redeem sinners.
Never confuse the price someone placed upon you with the dignity God bestowed upon you.
Never mistake another person's cruelty for God's verdict concerning your life.
And never allow the darkness you have witnessed to persuade you that darkness will ultimately win.
Revelation 21:4 points us toward the day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
Until that day, we must protect, speak, serve, pray, repent, and love.
We must remember the children.
We must remember the forgotten.
Above all, we must remember Jesus.
The world may have treated you as something to be sold, but your story was never theirs to own—and the evil written into your past does not have the authority to write your eternity.
